utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Glad to see that Mr. Sljivancanin is well enough to be back. Unfortunately, Judge Thelin is not, so that we will have to sit without him. Good morning, sir. Would you be kind enough to take the card and stand and read the affirmation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, I'll be asking you a number of questions on behalf of Mr. Mrksic's defence. There is one thing I'd like to ask you, though. Please follow the interpretation on the screen and when you see a sentence end, please make a pause to make it possible for the interpreters to interpret the proceedings and to keep the record accurate. First of all, can you please share your personal details with us, your full name, when were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Jaksic, I was born on the 2nd of November 1956, Babjak, Nasice municipality, Republic of Croatia. Father's name Dane. Anything else you want to know, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But can you please go slowly, sir, in answer to my questions? You speak very quickly and some of the information you've just shared with us has been lost in the process. Such as your place of birth, as far as I can see. So please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The village of Babjak, Nasice municipality, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. How long did you live there in the place you were born? Can you tell us about your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I lived in the village until 1971. I left for Vukovar to attend secondary school there. I completed my secondary education there and joined the army for my further schooling, the reserve officers school in Bileca. After completing the reserve officers school in Bileca, I did a term in Pirot. I was deputy commander for a reconnaissance platoon -- regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I suppose you're talking about the next stage of your military service. First of all, you completed your secondary education in Vukovar, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, immediately upon completion of your secondary education you joined the JNA for your regular military term?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had already turned 18 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please wait for me to finish my question before you start answering, first and foremost, and then after that, if you could please make another pause so that there is no overlap between questions and answers? Thank you, sir. You've already mentioned that you joined the JNA to go to the reserve officers school in Bileca. So my question is what sort of school is that and what sort of training did you receive there? Could anyone join that school or was there some sort of a selection process and who set the criteria for the selection process?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The reserve officers school in Bileca was the elite school for training officers in the former Yugoslavia. It provided the greatest and the best-trained officers and reserve officers. We did what you do at a military academy. Everything that the officers were taught at the military academy, we were taught at the reserve officers school although in an abbreviated form. This was for the land forces, infantry, specifically. But we received instruction in all the branches and the application of their skills. And we also received the training normally reserved for specialised units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The training took how long exactly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Seven months. A full seven months. Sometimes we would get two hours rest, but apart from that, everything else was studying, tactics and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Following this training, which as you say took seven months, which rank were you awarded and what happened later with your military service?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: After that, we received the rank of sergeant and we did our term with the various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Upon completing your training, did you all stay at the school in Bileca or were you deployed in various garrisons throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Some of us stayed at the school to continue to work with them and the rest were deployed all over the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, and you've spoken about this already, I think you mentioned Pirot as the next place you went. Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I spent the rest of my military term in Pirot. I was deputy commander of a reconnaissance platoon of the regiment. My commander was Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that you, as an officer, had subordinates?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you completed your military term, did you have a different rank by this time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Upon completing my military service, well, that depended on your commendations and on your merit. One could have been awarded the rank of Lieutenant; those who had proved their mettle. The same applied to the reserve officers school. Those who failed to meet the criteria could not progress past the rank of squad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As for you personally, how did you fare?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I got a job immediately. I reported for work and we had to report back in our place of birth. So I travelled back to Nasice to sign up and I found there the TO commander of Slovenia Baranja Zaponice, and the chief of security. The moment I came they wanted to have me appointed security organ in their battalion. However, I said I would only report there according to the rules but that I would continue to live in Vukovar and report there. And then Vukovar immediately received a reconnaissance platoon for the TO. It was a territorial brigade. I did a drill with them. We went from Vukovar to Nabrdje and completed a drill at Nabrdje. I was commended for my performance. I got a promotion and I was sent to do a security course and appointed a commander of the security -- of security at the Vukovar TO Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us which year this was when you completed your military service and reported -- well, what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was in June 1976 that I completed my military term, and I finally joined the army in April 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, that was your regular military term. But what you were talking about now was some sort of a continuation, wasn't it? Does that not mean that you turned professional, as it were? Or did you just continue to serve as a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I continued to serve as a reserve officer. It was a proper job, only in the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From mid-1976 on, when you returned from your regular military term of duty, you had a regular job and continued to work in Vukovar, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Cazmatrans company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did you live at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In Vukovar. As soon as the decision was taken to grant me permanent employment, I bought some land and a house. I lived with my brother until I got married. When I got married, I did a make-over in that house and I moved in straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From that time on, say up to 1991, did you live and work in Vukovar all the time with no major interruptions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us about the course in Pancevo and all that. Ever since 1976, which was the end of your military term and all the way up until 1991, in your capacity as a reserve officer, what were you required to do in terms of training, drills, that sort of thing? Can you share that with us, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: While I was commander of the reconnaissance platoon of the brigade, I went through all the drills for special units, reconnaissance units, and for military police units. Later, when I became chief of security, I spent a month in Pancevo doing the security course and then in Erdut, Rakijica, doing other courses. And I was with all the brigade's battalions doing military drills. I would always be there helping them or in an official capacity or sometimes as a referee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What exactly did that mean? Was this Territorial Defence? Was this something else? Would you tell us about how this was organised?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: A TO were the reserve forces of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. This was organised along military lines in terms of units, platoons, squads and then up to corps level. It comprised all the regulation weapons for anti-infantry combat, for antitank combat and for anti-air force combat. The only thing they didn't have were rocket systems and armoured equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether the TO was thus structured throughout the territory of Yugoslavia or was this specific to the area you were resident at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It is true that the TO was organised in the same way throughout Yugoslavia. The TO units were financed by the municipalities in which territories they lay. If the municipality had more resources then the TO unit would be better equipped. And vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I see. The level of equipment achieved in these respective TO units could vary from municipality to municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as your TO unit in Vukovar is concerned, how did it rank in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Vukovar TO brigade was one of the best equipped and the best-trained such units in the area of Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the makeup of the TO brigade? Was it multi-ethnic? Did it reflect the ethnic makeup of the population in the area or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The brigade consisted of all the ethnicities present in the area. Depending on the part of the municipality, the units makeup could differ, again reflecting the population. We could have one battalion from the north, one from northwest, the other one from southeast. It was on this territorial municipal basis that the brigade was formed. If there were insufficient levels of manpower, specifically officers, then they would be recruited from other parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about the differing compositions of units depending on the area they hailed from and we had witnesses testifying about that already. We know -- my question to you is whether the makeup of the population in Vukovar and in the area was mixed or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called Vukovar a Yugoslavia in miniature. There were 28 different ethnicities and minorities living in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Serbs. Only Serbs and people from mixed marriages declared themselves as Yugoslavs. They were, I believe, around 8 per cent, and then the most represented were Serbs and then Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You're saying that people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs in your opinion were actually Serbs declaring themselves as such?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course, there were quite a few Croats too. All things considered, could you say that the Croat and Serb population were more or less equally represented or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, there were 49 per cent of Serbs and around I think 6 per cent of Yugoslavs. Then, well, you can see which ethnic group was in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You're talking about Vukovar. Now what about the villages around Vukovar? Were there villages that were almost mono-ethnic, Croat, Serb or Hungarian villages and were there villages that were multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were villages that were up to 99 per cent mono-ethnic and of course there were those that were multi-ethnic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this why, when you talked about the makeup of the TO brigade, the ethnic makeup of these units differed depending on the area they hailed from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: From platoons, companies, and up to battalions, you would have some ethnicities more represented than others but at any rate, these units always reflected the ethnic makeup of the population in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us the training you underwent, also within the TO, and you said that you were also a referee during one of these drills. Can you explain this for us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This meant that this person was to follow the drill itself with particular reference on the tactics applied, the command and control structures and all of these different areas were then graded. It also involved the advisory aspect of it, in terms of this person then giving recommendations to the participants in the drill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's to say that this referee was there in order to evaluate and grade the participants in the drill?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In that period where it seems to me you held a particularly important role in the Vukovar TO brigade, did the events take their course in the same way up until the year 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible. In the years 1990 and 1991, what was typical of Croatia and specifically Vukovar? Did something prominent happen in the second half of 1990 in Croatia and Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: With the multi-party elections and the rise of the HDZ to power, the situation changed radically. Vukovar was no longer the town it used to be. One did not feel free any longer. There was no more equality in society. There was apprehension at workplaces. With the rise of the HDZ to power, the municipal building in Vukovar was shot at. It had been for decades before that the Cyrillic sign stood on that building without ever being attacked. Croats started avoiding contact with Serbs. They started separating themselves from them. Then in Bogdanovci there was an armed group that got organised and there was another thing that boded that things would not be well and there was the arming of Croatia from Hungary. This involved Spegelj and these people who were involved in that should have been arrested right away but this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please go slowly. We want your testimony to be reflected in the transcript. I will go back to your answer because it was quite a long one. Were you talking about the period I asked about, that's to say, the second half of 1990 and the first half of 1991 when you talked about these events?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have a question involving this incident concerning the sign and the coat of arms. Can you explain for us what happened? You said that this coat of arms with the Cyrillic inscription had been there for many years. Was it part of tradition? Was there a time when the Cyrillic script was used more frequently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: During the Austro-Hungarian empire the Serbs got their autonomy, their script, their schools and their national identity. In the area of Vojvodina, which was the then Krajina, meaning the area dividing Austro-Hungarian empire from Turkey, from the Ottoman empire, the Serbs formed the army in this zone and they had their rights. At that point in time, the Cyrillic script started being used. They had their religious facilities and schools and all the other elements that a proper nation has in its own right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The coat of arms that was placed on the front of that building had been there for years and it was at this point that it became damaged?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In the Serb script, you spell JA separately, just as in the Croat script. However, this particular coat of arms contained the letter "J" written in the Russian form, which serves to show how long back in history it dated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned this incident as one of the incidents that made the population upset and anxious. Do you know of any other such incidents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was gun-fire on Serb homes, and on Serb establishments, Serb establishments were being blown-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say Serb, what exactly do you mean? Are you referring to the fact that these establishments were owned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. These incidents were directed against the Serbs who owned such establishments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were such incidents ever the subject of prosecution by the then courts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. These incidents were actually perpetrated by the members of the MUP because they were part of the state-orchestrated terror organised by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Had not the MUP itself up to that point been a multi-ethnic institution reflecting the ethnic makeup of the population?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Up until the victory of the HDZ, the MUP had been multi-ethnic. At the point of the change in government, the ethnic makeup in the MUP changed to the benefit of the Croats. I will tell you that one -- only one combat vehicle in Vukovar was better-equipped than the entire MUP in Vinkovci. However, the seat of the MUP which used to be in Vukovar was relocated to Vinkovci, thereby making the office in Vukovar only a branch office. The intention was to have Vinkovci run the entire personnel policy, finances and the entire wherewithal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know when this came about and why?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It occurred alongside the victory of the HDZ, or rather, the HDZ did not win the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that it did not win, what do you mean, in Croatia or --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know what the situation was like in Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The HDZ won in Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you well, it was the HDZ that won in Croatia. That's something that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you believe that this was, in fact, the reason why the head office of the MUP was relocated from Vukovar to Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that you're talking about the change of the ethnic makeup in the MUP, did it involve the recruitment of Croats into their ranks or were they recruited from other parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At that point in time they increasingly started employing persons who were under constant supervision of MUP who had been vetted by MUP. These were persons whose personal record was terrible. They were former convicts. They had been prosecuted and had such track records as would never ever previously permit them to be employed in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Up until 1991, such persons who were former convicts or had police records were -- would they ever be employed by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. One always vetted them thoroughly going back to their fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfather, to double check that these were persons of integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on what you say, at the point the HDZ came to power in Croatia, a change in -- of policy took place where such persons with criminal records were being employed by the MUP. Can you tell us what the ethnicity of these persons was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, they were almost entirely Croats, and people who were loyal to the HDZ and the HDZ policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any attempts at changing the police uniform of the MUP at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Not at first, while they still had uniforms in stock. It was gradually that they started changing their uniforms which were similar to military uniforms but they were blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could one notice a greater presence of the police in the streets of Vukovar and could it in any way be compared to the pre-election period in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The makeup of the police had changed. The manpower had been multiplied. None of the incidents inflicted on the local Serbs were ever resolved and no charges were brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say no one was prosecuted and the perpetrators were never found, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It's not that the perpetrators were unknown. The perpetrators were among them but they were not prepared to take any steps against those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anyone do anything about it in an organised manner or individually?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was nothing anyone could do. As I said a while ago, the HDZ had never won the elections in Vukovar but they were effectively in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How did that come about? How was it possible that the local authorities were made up of those who actually had won the elections?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There had been two parties originally in the running.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say two parties, I assume --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The HDZ -- I mean two major parties -- and the League of Communists, then known as the SDP. The Serbs and non-Croats mostly voted communist and SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: SDP, what did that mean? What did that stand for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: League of democratic change.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: SKH, SDP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who led that party?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Ivica Racan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He is a Croat who contributed the most to the HDZ sweeping win in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How exactly did he do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: When the assembly was set up, between the SDF or the League of Communists or the HDZ, all those who were there, the candidates, and over 50 of those were Croats in the League of Communists, everybody automatically switched to the HDZ and voted in their platform and their statute instead of supporting their own League of Communists, so that the majority party became effectively marginalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the SDP was both a Croat and a Serb party which means that it counted among its membership both Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, same as the League of Communists. They kept the name in order to fool the Serbs because they thought they were voting the Croatian League of Communists but actually they were pro-HDZ and Racan and the rest of them, the alleged communists, effectively handed over power entirely to the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's just go a while back. What about the election platform of the HDZ? -- of the SDP, was that a nationalist one or was it pro-Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Pre1974, there was the League of Communists, the Yugoslav League of Communists, and 1974 is the watershed because it then turned nationalist because the republics all had their own parties now. So now this was Croatia's League of Communists which means that to some extent it did have a more ethnic feature to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I understand. But in terms of the platform, was it any different from the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was different. It was a platform for the entire population. It was not extremely nationalistic or anything. It was in favour of unity. Brotherhood and unity were the catch words at the time for all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia. So the platform of the former League of Communists, Yugoslavia's League of Communists was to some extent preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it wasn't the platform that constituted the real problem. The problem was most of those in the party's list who were elected immediately joined the other side. They switched sides.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were like a Trojan horse. The Serbs never had their own ethnic party. They were always pro-Yugoslav and that's why they placed their trust in the League of Communists because the League of Communists always struggled to preserve Yugoslavia as a whole. However, they had their own Croat candidates, and after the elections, all those who had been members of the League of Communists were now joining the HDZ. They declared a majority in the assembly and the Serbs no longer had any say in the government, in the town's assembly or in the Croatian parliament for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, at the time the Serbs did not have their own national party. You say that most of them were members of the SDP believing all the while that this party would be the best choice to protect their interests, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was telling you about the town of Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you did say that in Vukovar, this party had a majority. Who was the president of the Municipal Assembly after the elections?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He was a Serb, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there anything he could do in order to improve the situation of the non-Croats living in the area, because if I understand you correctly, you imply that all the other non-Serbs felt the same fear on account of the growing Croatian nationalism, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think Slavko Dokmanovic was the only president in the whole of Europe who was a municipality president but had no real power, and he was reduced to saving his own neck eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please explain that in the briefest possible terms? What do you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As municipality president, the majority party, when the Croats switched over to the HDZ, he no longer had a majority to run in the assembly. Later on, I heard from people who had worked with him how they ran for their lives and how they were -- how they were looking for him and his son in order to have them killed and they looked for them all over but these people helped him hide and get away from these people who were looking for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was he president of the Municipal Assembly or chairman of the Municipal Assembly until the end of his term of office?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, he did not remain all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember why?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He wasn't able to, for reasons of personal safety. He wasn't even allowed to come anywhere near the Municipal Assembly building later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say he wasn't even allowed later to come to Vukovar, he didn't come to the municipality building, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And what remained of the Serbs in the assembly was a mere handful. Everything else had been taken over by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you specify the time period at least roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was quite a while ago. It's been 15 years. I didn't meddle into politics because I just wasn't interested in politics at the time. All I cared about was my work, my family. I was just an ordinary citizen. I wasn't into politics because I simply wasn't interested at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were not a party member? You were not a member of any party? You did not hold any post in any of the parties and you did not run in the municipal elections, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you remember who replaced Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think his name was Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there another election or did happen differently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, it was outside of an election.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the outset you answered some questions about these changes that affected the population in Vukovar municipality and its surroundings. You talked about your work and the problems you faced there. What sort of problems at work, these have been stemming from the things you just described?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: When the HDZ came to power, the MUP made it patently clear to all the Croats that they would now be allowed to receive weapons with no background checks or anything. So whoever applied to receive weapons was entitled to. There were no checks, no vetting. It was a matter of your first and last name. If you were a Croat, you were given a weapon or you were given a permit to purchase a weapon. If not, not. For example, if there were 100 or 200 or 500 applications, maybe a Serb or two would slip through the cracks but the Croats were receiving these permits a on massive scale, even underage children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the time period preceding the first multi-party elections which is the bulk of the time you spent in Vukovar. What was the procedure for obtaining a weapon under the law? Were citizens entitled to apply for permits and how were they vetted? Were any background checks run?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was possible but it was very difficult to obtain these permits. Those who were granted their permits needed a good reason. You needed to have a squeaky clean record and you had to be of impeccable mental health to be granted a weapon. Very few people were ever granted these permits. For the most part, it was on account of the nature of their jobs. For example, if these people needed a weapon for reason as of personal safety but it was nearly impossible for just an ordinary citizen, a man in the street, to obtain a permit for obtaining a weapon. It was hardly ever the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. So that was the procedure applied under the law, if I understand you correctly, and this was applied in practice, wasn't it? My question, however, is: What kind of weapons were citizens entitled to receive legally?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The only way was for a citizen to be a member of a hunters' association or a marksman, a competing marksman. Military officers were entitled to own a weapon and persons professionally involved in security, the police, for example, but they had their own regulation weapons, but they could still keep those, hold on to those, once they retired, if a special permit was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you speak about hunters, the permits were probably in relation to hunting weapons. What about ordinary citizens, what kind of weapons could they possibly have been granted?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Pistols and revolvers, only those two kinds, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about rifles, semi-automatic, automatic? Could anything like that ever end up in the hands of an ordinary citizen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, not legally. Permits weren't issued for that. Trophy weapons alone, those actually not meant to be used but kept as trophies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. You spoke about some incidents and you spoke about attacks on buildings and buildings being booby trapped. What about these explosives? Was it possible to come by such explosives legally at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But were explosives used in these incidents that started occurring at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They first booby trapped the kiosk near the barracks to keep the army from receiving the daily press. They booby trapped it twice, and blew it up and the explosives used were quite powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say the kiosk near the barracks, it was probably where the soldiers got their newspapers, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's not right next to the barracks but it's nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say booby trapped, that doesn't necessarily mean that the explosive was used to blow up the kiosk. Was it ever blown up eventually?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, not the kiosk itself. The nearby buildings were damaged too because the explosive used was very powerful. The power lines were damaged and the pylons and the windows and roofs on the surrounding buildings. That's how strong the explosion was, how powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the exact time when this occurred, how long before the real clashes broke out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I think by this time Croats had already erected a number of barricades along certain roads, along the roads leading into Vukovar. Not in the town itself at this time but I remember near the Djergaj warehouse which was near the Cazmatrans company headquarters which is where I worked. They set up obstacles, mines, anti-tank mines, and set up electric systems of explosives along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'll be asking you more about the barricades a little later on. You said they set all those things up. Who exactly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps, the ZNG, and the MUP, Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What exactly was the National Guards Corps, since you mentioned them as distinct from the MUP? Was that the same thing? Was that similar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This was a new unit that had never existed before. This was something organised by Tudjman and the HDZ. It was outside the Yugoslav army, outside the TO, outside the armed forces. In addition to these or outside these, they set up their own National Guards Corps, which bore all the Ustasha insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it an armed military formation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had uniforms, camouflage uniforms, and on their chest pocket they had large Us standing for the Ustasha movement. They did not have any caps. They had bandanas and bayonets and their boots and they were frightful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you mentioned the chest pocket with the letter U. Was it something resembling a U or did it really stand for the Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a U, and beneath it was written the Ustasha rebirth. I was on my way to work and at that point of the Djergaj forest, I saw a uniformed person approaching another person and harassing the person because they thought that the person was a Serb. He was a Croat. So there was this one MUP member there who tried to ID the Croat who was there. There was this Zenga member who came over and started harassing him under the impression that he was a Serb. He seemed to be holding a kind of a prominent position among them. The question was put, "Have you brushed your teeth?" And the man answered, "Why?" What they meant was of course that he had bad breath because he was a Serb but then once they realised they were mistaken that the man was a Croat, they let him go and we were allowed past. Had it not been for the two of them, I don't think I would have escaped alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you well, first there was this MUP member who checked persons and then --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, those who were Serbs were handed over to the other ones. This police officer was an elderly man. The police officers who had been in the MUP even before the changes took place, they referred to the new ones as Franjo's men because of course he meant Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On page 23, line 4, it says that the man was a member of Zenga. Of course, what you meant was that he was a Zenga, a member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this particular incident an isolated event or were there more such incidents and did they become an ordinary occurrence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Before this incident, Jovan Jakovljevic was killed. Zeljko Pajic simply disappeared. He was our neighbour. He went to town to get supplies for his shop. His car was found parked in front of the municipal building. It was full of drinks that he had procured for his shop. He was taken away by Mercep, never to be seen again. This spring, a dead body was found in the Danube River, and a DNA test was carried out on the body, and it was established that this was indeed the man. His mother had been trying to retrieve his body for years but it was only this year that they managed to do this. There was another ethnic Hungarian whose house had come under attack and who was killed. He was not a Croat and was therefore killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the full names of these persons? Because they were not entered correctly in the transcript, probably because you went quite quickly. Can you tell us who these persons were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Jovan Jakovljevic also known as Rakijica. Zeljko Pajic from Nova Ulica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Zeljko, the person who went missing and whose identity has been recently established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm sure I heard you mention a family name Mercep. I'm just trying to see whether I can find it in the transcript. Yes. Who is Mercep?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Mercep was a construction technician who worked in Borovo before the war, but he was a HDZ activist. He was setting up what were purported to be unarmed detachments of the HDZ, which were in fact armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he officially hold position in the town at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: He represented himself as the commander of the TO Vukovar staff. He was stationed at the TO headquarters near to the municipal building. There is a nuclear shelter there which was allegedly his torture chamber. After the liberation of Vukovar, the nuclear shelter was found to be smeared with blood, the walls covered with blood stains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We will come to that period later. We are talking about the period shortly before the outbreak of the conflicts and the period that was marked by these increasing incidents. It was at that period of time that I wanted to know what he did. Was there a Secretariat for National Defence in existence at the time in Vukovar as apparently it was in all the other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but it worked until the rise to power of the HDZ, at which point all the Serbs who used to work there were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The man you mentioned, Mercep, did he have a role to play in this Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Do you mean before the war or right before the war or, rather, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will repeat it. At any point in time before the outbreak of hostilities, did Mercep have a role to play in the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of conflicts, he took complete charge of the Secretariat. Serbs had to ask for permits to allow them free movement. As soon as there were roadblocks, they did not dare move around. His groups were active throughout the town. I don't know all their names. I don't know all these persons but there were many Serbs who went missing before the conflicts actually broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You just mentioned passes or permits for free movement. Was it necessary to have passes to move into and out of town before the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. It was provided that only in the areas affected by the war, such passes would be required. This was not a time of war, but nevertheless, he had to be consulted if one wanted to go into town or out of town. Even a MP who was a Croat had to first see him in order to be allowed to leave town to attend a parliamentary session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me, did it have any bearing on the ordinary citizens who had to go to work every day and then back home?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, people were harassed at their workplace, simply because they were Serbs. They were fired. Croats openly walked around with belts and pistols tucked at the belts. Some even had as many as two pistols tucked at their belts. And you can imagine what their life was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you knew that some persons who were Serbs simply went missing. You also mentioned an ethnic Hungarian. Were people leaving Vukovar at the time, individually and whole families?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As soon as these events started occurring, whoever had a place to go to left to Serbia or even to the seaside, whoever had a place to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you personally leave Vukovar at the time or did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: My family left. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me, I believe I haven't asked you this: What part of town did you live in at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I lived at Sajmiste at the time. This was later renamed Petrova Gora because a street there is called Petrova Gora and this was the part of town that we organised for our uses. It's an area -- a perimeter of around 500 to 700 metres that was referred to Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How many streets were covered by this area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Petrova Gora, Solidarnost, Radnicka street, a part of Radnicka street, a part of Solidarnost. A part of Svetozar Markovic street, and about one fourth of Nova street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of this neighbourhood, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was multi-ethnic but with a Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me go back to one of your earlier answers. You talked about people moving out and you said that your personal family -- your own family left and you said that many families went to the seaside. Were you referring only to the families of Serb ethnicities and other ethnicities or did this include Croats too?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At the time Mercep started erecting roadblocks. All the families who had a place to go to moved out, including Serbs, Croats and others. They realised that there was terror on the streets, that we were being pushed into a ghetto.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that passes were being issued. You said who issued them and in what way. Where were these passes checked? I suppose there had to be a place where one had to present these passes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: At all the exits of the town there were check-points erected, and it was members of the MUP and ZNG who checked the passes. Nobody was allowed to leave town who did not have a pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the same applied to entering the town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned these roadblocks a while ago. Were all these check-points manned by members of the MUP and ZNG or were there any other roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were roadblocks erected at the streets that were peripheral along the edge of town. For instance, Svetozar Markovic had two roadblocks or check-points. There was Nova street that also had two check-points and this was something that I was surprised to see, that we should also have check-points in the downtown area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, initially these check-points were erected along the perimeter of the town but later on check-points were erected to separate two areas, two neighbourhoods in a town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Perhaps you don't know because you did not leave Vukovar at the time, but do you know what was going on in the area around Vukovar? You said this morning that there were villages with a predominant Serb population or a Croat population and that there were mixed villages in the hinterland of Vukovar. Do you know what the situation was like there specifically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: My wife and my children, I have four children, left Vukovar in July. My children went through a horrific experience. One cannot believe that. They were going across a check-point to Serbia. At every entrance and exit to every single village there were ZNG members who went on the bus and checked the passengers for men. If they found any men then they took them off these buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that this was in July. I suppose we know which year that was but can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You explained the direction your family took when leaving Vukovar. You said they went across Ilok. Which were these villages that they went through?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Ilok is the town to the south of Vukovar along the Danube River. On the head land of Fruska Gora. From Ilok to Backa Palanka, there was a bridge across the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about Ilok and the surrounding villages, what was the population there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Predominantly Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke in great detail about the TO, about the TO Brigade, from 1976 onwards, about how it was organised. How did all these developments affect the very existence of that brigade? Was the TO Brigade, as it had been known up to then, still in existence at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The weapons and equipment belonging to the TO were stored in military warehouses in the Djergaj forest or in the barracks. All of our files belonging to units and other bodies were kept in the TO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You're talking about the headquarters that --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was taken over by Mercep. It was from this headquarters the Secretariat for All People's Defence that recruitment was carried out, and that call-ups were being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did this still apply at the time? Was recruitment being done the same way as before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. The TO Brigade was disbanded and units of the National Guards Corps and MUP units were now set up to be used as their own armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When talking about the Territorial Brigade you also mentioned your position, your role. You were a commander, weren't you? One thing I didn't ask you was, did you get a promotion in terms of your rank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I had become reserve captain by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As a reserve captain, were you ever called up by the TO? Did you receive any assignments and what about your other Serb mates?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. None of the Serbs were called up or mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that not mean that the Territorial Brigade had ceased to exist or perhaps it continued to exist under a different guise?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: On paper it existed all right. It's just that it wasn't operating. The brigade members still had their uniforms at home, the full kit that they had signed for. They still kept those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this all right under the law for members of the reserve forces to keep their uniforms at home?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was perfectly legitimate. All the reserve members did that. As soon as they received call-ups, you would turn up at the collection point already wearing a uniform and then the unit would deploy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume you too had a uniform, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The uniform of a reserve officer, a reserve captain, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say you were not called up again for military drills or mobilised for that matter. Do you perhaps remember the last time you went to a military drill and how did that work exactly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Last one was just before the multi-party elections, before the emergence of the HDZ. I can't be more specific. But were I to consult my military booklet, perhaps I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know if any units were organised along party lines, armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The HDZ supplied the whole of the Croatian population there. While I was still working, whenever I got off the bus I could tell immediately which village had received weapons and which had received none. You got off the bus and you saw the locals gloating, saying that they had received their weapons and that weapons had already been distributed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, they displayed these weapons and some people told you stories as you were passing through. It wasn't something that could go unobserved. It was an open secret virtually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say weapons, which weapons are we looking at? The same weapons that were allowed before the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. Now they had Kalashnikovs, pistols, machine-guns, all the different types of small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say this is something that was done by the HDZ, a political party. How was this possible? Was it strictly along party lines or was this organised by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This was organised by the top-most leadership of Croatia, the top party leadership, so this was torture inflicted by bodies of the Croatian state against all the non-Croats and specifically Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I think you said it yourself, didn't you, you were saying that TO weapons were stored in certain TO warehouses or in the JNA barracks. What about these weapons? According to your account, these weapons had not come from those sources but from a different source. Do you know how they got to be there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The weapons came in through Hungary. When the first video was aired about Spegelj and them transporting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about a film that the RTS published at one point with the then General Spegelj agreeing on something?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No I'm talking about the trucks on the border that were filmed carrying weapons and there was even a plane that landed in Zagreb carrying weapons and equipment. This plane was later intercepted by the army and both the plane and the weapons were seized but that was at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. When you talked about Hungary, that isn't quite clear. You talked about these films of weapons crossing the border from Hungary illegally, I suppose, into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I think this might be the perfect time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will resume at 10 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we have no prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Domazet. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, let's pick up where we left off. I will ask you now or, rather, you were talking before the break about barricades across Vukovar, on the roads leading out of Vukovar. And now a subject which I will tackle briefly, the JNA, more specifically, the Vukovar barracks during this period. Do you know what became of the JNA barracks at this time, or more generally, do you know what became of the JNA's armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was an engineers' battalion stationed in the Vukovar barracks, the JNA battalion, they also kept watch on the Djergaj warehouse and when the riots started there was a platoon that was securing the bridge at Erdut. A vehicle which shuttled back and forth every day carrying food to those at Djergaj and those at the Erdut bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know how things worked with the JNA and the barracks? Were they allowed through at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, just across the way from the Cazmatrans company is the Djergaj warehouse, so you need to cross that road about a hundred metres into the woods. There was a barricade there with road obstacles, huge concrete pyramids, anti-tank mines. So this was a barricade for military vehicles, not for civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say for military vehicles, what you mean is this barricade was erected to stop military vehicles from passing, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. When a military vehicle drove up, it would have to slow down to about ten kilometres per hour in order to successfully negotiate all the curves through that barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about the Cazmatrans company, and this being nearby. Wasn't that your company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 156 brought up on our monitors? This is a map of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If you could please have a look, sir, and try to point out some of the things that I'm about to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Djergaj warehouse is in the direction of Brsadin village. On the left-hand side of the road is the Djergaj forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in slightly or, rather, zoom out. That's fine. A little less please because I think we are now losing sight of another area that is material to us, a bit higher up, please, higher up, up. Pull it up because we need Brsadin and the road to Brsadin. Lower down, down, down, down. No, actually we need to --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We need the upper portion of the map, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, what is it that you wanted to indicate on the map? I think you were talking about Djergaj, right? You will be given a pen that you will use to mark things on the map.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This is the military warehouse called Djergaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle around it, please, and use a number 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This is the Djergaj forest and this is the military warehouse known as Djergaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please just circle it and put a number 1 there? Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Right there in the middle of this grove or woods. My own company, the Cazmatrans, is here at the Vukovar-Brsadin road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please put a number 2 there and circle it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The barricade was right outside Cazmatrans where the Medica warehouse used to be. They stored medicines there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please mark the barricade, put a B there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: In the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we see on this map the area you described as Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, not on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It's further down, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the way down. It's in the south of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While we are using this portion of the map, if you can please mark other barricades that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were barricades at the entry point into Vukovar along the Trpinje-Vukovar road. Number 3. There was one on the way to Borovo Selo, a large barricade. There was a cafe there. Around the mid-point along that road there was a large barricade there, and that's where the first military vehicle was booby trapped, around these parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about a cafe. There were witnesses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers kindly be asked to speak one at a time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Number 3 is near the Zurich cafe and number 4 is near the Slon cafe, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If we could please scroll down a little, or rather, maybe it's better in order not to lose these, perhaps, we should have this admitted into evidence and then get a blank map, this same one, but without the markings on our monitors, if possible, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this map will become Exhibit 766.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have Exhibit 156, that is the same map, but without the markings? And if we could please blow up the portion just underneath where it says Nova Ulica? Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, do you see the area that you described as --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No. This only has Brsadin and it doesn't have the entire road. A bit of the road is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm talking about Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please mark the area you described as Petrova Gora, but the general area, because you were explaining about those streets and parts of streets. Mark to the best of your recollection the boundaries of that area which you refer to as Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I'll mark the streets where our security were holding. Petrova Gora street, that's the one. Solidarnost street, Svetozar Markovica street, this part up to here. And this section of Nova street, this stretch, thereabouts. These roughly speaking were the boundaries of Petrova Gora that was under our control and we were keeping Mercep's forces out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does this represent the external boundaries of Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the boundary that we were controlling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Put a number 1 there, please. So this is Petrova Gora. Can you please tell me where the barricades were that you spoke about earlier as being in this area, in this neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was one at Svetozar Markovica but further down, their barricade. There was another one at Svetozar Markovica and there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please use crosses to mark the places where the barricades were set up? Could you encircle that cross, please, and put a number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: And a number 3 up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The number 3 barricade was on the way to Bogdanovci but that doesn't matter. I'm drawing the ones in Petrova Gora and around. There was another one at Vuteks, number 4. There was another one on the way to Negoslavci in this neighbourhood, number 5. These were the barricades around us. There was another one at the far end of Nova street, Proleterska street. At the junction here, another barricade, the junction of Proleterska and Carsivanja. All the junctions were blocked by barricades in actual fact. But these were the largest ones where they used pallets of bricks, anti-infantry and anti-tank mines to keep people from crossing. This is where their check-points were. MUP and ZNG check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You used numbers 2 to 5 or 6 to mark the significant check-points held by the ZNG and MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what about downtown?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Downtown they had fortifications with sandbags in all the important institutions in the town, like the SDK building, the children's health centre. Whenever I passed through that part of town, that was where I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that's quite enough for this part of the neighbourhood you inhabited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence under a separate number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this marked map will become Exhibit 767.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't made a marking in respect of Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this same exhibit, 156, be enlarged a bit so as to show the barracks as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, do you see this part of town?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the barracks has not been correctly entered, plotted into the map because the dot is not where the barracks was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean the red dot. Could you please use a little cross to mark the exact location of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Just circle it and mark with number 1. In your opinion, the barracks is a bit lower than marked here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, because this is the rough location of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about Velepromet, is it approximately the right location?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about Nova Ulica? Of course, it cannot be a single dot, seeing it's a street.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, no. This isn't the right location of Nova Ulica. Can I draw a line? It starts from the railway track and -- here, this line is Nova Ulica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please mark it with number 2. This will be part of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As regards the part of town where the JNA barracks was, do you know whether there were any roadblocks there, check-points, and what their location was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: On the way out, in the direction of Negoslavci, somewhere in the direction of Negoslavci where the houses peter out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please would you mark that location.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any check-points around the barracks itself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The ZNG laid mines around the barracks by using anti-tank mines and anti-personnel land mines. Fortunately, they were not really skillful with the activation so there weren't many explosions. This is where the mines were, and the ZNG members occupied all the houses around the barracks and the barracks itself was constantly under mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The area you marked as the minefield, could you please mark it with number 4.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this map be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this map will become Exhibit 768.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We won't be needing the map any more. Perhaps we will use it later on to make some markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, as you explained, you were staying in the area called Petrova Gora where your house is; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You and your closest and dearest ones, who were in that neighbourhood, did you start organising yourselves when these check-points were erected?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We started once the Croats were arming themselves. We cooped up all the weapons we had. Some of us had hunting weapons, others had home-made weapons like I had, an old-fashioned pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please explain for the Trial Chamber this old-fashioned pistol Kubura, what it was, in fact, although I do see that it is entered in the transcript that it was an old-fashioned pistol?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a home-made type of -- more of a rifle, really, which -- or rather, it looks like a pistol but it uses the ammunition of a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We were not that afraid of the Mercep group in daytime. We were afraid of their groups arriving at night. That was why we had local village guards. As these check-points were already erected and they had already armed themselves, we were by that time already surrounded, we were unable to reach the area where the shops were. There were civilians fleeing to the barracks, and the army itself managed to evacuate 2.000 people who had initially sought shelter in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This will be a separate topic that we will deal with. I will be asking you about the barracks and about the people who found refuge there. Now would you please explain what it was that you were doing at Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: As a group of citizens who were afraid and feared for their families and properties, we organised ourselves under a military principle, along a military principle, into village guards. We established squads by streets which had squad commanders. Each commander was given an area to take care of. We briefed them on the way normally the ZNG members raid the area, the way they carry out attacks. We developed a defence strategy, and we also envisaged a way the possible evacuation or reinforcements would be made in the event of a attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The unit that was organised in your street, who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which way did you come to be the commander of the unit? Did anyone appoint you or give you such an order?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: This was self-organisation. As I was the one who had the most military knowledge, I was chosen among the group to be the commander. I was chosen by the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there anyone who held a higher rank than yours in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that your rank at the time was that of a reserve captain?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The other persons you mentioned, who were under your command, were they also able-bodied men who had their military service, or -- and were there any elderly among you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: We had all served our military term. There were no underage persons among us because I didn't want to have children there. They were all members of the TO. They all wore uniforms. We made sure that we had uniforms on in order to be able to recognise our lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that all those under your command were members of the TO structure from before and had had uniforms assigned to them which they kept at home?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall how many people were under your command in that time period, this unit, I don't know how you referred to it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: By the 14th of September, we had around 180 people organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All of them were natives of the area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were several of them who came from outside the town. There were those who came from Mitnica to help us defend that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Most of the people who were in your unit were actually living in that part of town but there were also others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were others who were unable to leave the town but had come to join us from other parts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us why these people were unable to leave the town and decided to join you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: These people wanted to evacuate their families but, as these large check-points had already been established along the edge of town, they were unable to go past these and instead, following small lanes, reached our part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us why this was so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Serbs did not organise themselves in any way. Whoever was able to simply fled for life and that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Out of 180 people who were there, were they all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were even Croats, Ruthenians, Ukrainians, and other ethnic minorities and of course there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say that there were even Croats among you. This is a bit strange. How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: They were neighbours of ours. These Croats were in favour of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, they joined you on a voluntary basis, they didn't want to abandon their homes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned a date a while ago. I believe it was the 14th of September. You said up until the 14th of September. I suppose that's in 1991. But why did you mention that date? In particular, why is it important?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: It was on the 14th of September that we headed to lift the blockade of the barracks. They had been under blockade for a long time, their electricity and water supplies were cut off. They were unable to leave the barracks. They were under constant fire from infantry and artillery fire, as the barracks itself was situated in the midst of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know who was to be found in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
utterances.text: There was a military unit there and around 50 to 60 Vukovar residents who were volunteers. They went to the barracks and decided to lend them a hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about people, women and children, in the barracks. What was this all about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC
